body_ar:
لقد قدمت لأحد المشايخ طلبا لطريقته فأعطانيها مصحوبة بشروط منها الأخذ بالجد و العهد والكتمان وألا أخل بالشرط وبالتوحيد و بالفرائض وأنا أجهل العلم فبقيت بذالك على الطريق وخدمة الشيخ حتى توفي فتعودت الزيارة بالوقار والدعاء و بعد ذالك أتوسل إلى الله بأعماله الصالحة كما كنت أتوسل به حيا لاكتساب المنافع وإزالة الأضرار فهل هذا من السنة أو من الشرك أعاذنا الله؟ إن هذه النصائح التي نصحه بها الشيخ لا غبار عليها فعلى الإنسان أن يأخذ بالجد وأن يفي بالعهد وكذلك أن لا يخل بالتوحيد ولا بالفرائض و أن يتعلم العلم فهذه النصائح تجب على الشيخ أن ينصح بها ويجب أيضا على المنصوح أن ينصح بها دائما

فقد قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «الدين النصيحة قلنا لمن قال لله ولكتابه ولرسوله ولأئمة المسلمين و عامتهم» وبالنسبة لما ذكره أنه يجهل العلم فإن مجرد الأذكار التي يؤديها لا تغني عن طلب العلم بل يلزم الإنسان أن يتعلم ما جاء به النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لعل ما يفعله أصلا مخالف لما جاء به النبي صلى الله عليه و سلم فليبحث عما جاء به النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وليعمل به وليجعله حكما على كل ما سواه فإن كان ما أمر به الشيخ أو غيره موافقا لما جاء به النبي صلى الله عليه و سلم فليعمل به الإنسان لأن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أمره به وإن كان مخالفا لشيء جاء به النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فليرده على صاحبه كائنا من كان ولا يستحيي أن يرد على أحد شيئا خالف ما جاء به النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم حتى لو كان والدا أو شيخا أو كبيرا فلا يمكن أن تأخذ خلاف ما أتى به النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم من عند أي أحد. بالنسبة لما يفعله هذا الشخص بعد موت الشيخ المذكور من الزيارة فإن زيارة القبور مندوبة عموما للمسلمين لتذكر الآخرة لكنها لا ينتفع بها المزور ولا يدركها ولا يحس بها أصلا ولا يسمع شيئا مما يقوله الزائر ولا يمكن أن ينفعه بأي شيء لا يرفع عنه ضررا ولا يجلب له نفعا وليس بينهما أية علاقة وإنما تتعظ بعظامه التي تأكلها الأرض وتتعظ بأسراره و أمواله التي صارت ملكا لغيره وتتعظ بأهله الذين كانوا يظنون أنه ينفعهم ويقوم بأمورهم وقد ذهب عنهم فلم يضرهم شيئا فهذا الذي يحصل لك من زيارة أي قبر من القبور وزيارة القبور سواء كان أصحابها أهل إيمان أو أهل كفر أو أهل صلاح أو أهل فسق أو تعرفهم أو لا تعرفهم تؤدي إلى هذا التذكر تذكر الآخرة و هذا المطلوب منها وأما الأموات فإنما ينتفعون في قبورهم بالدعاء أن تدعوا لهم وإذا دعوت لهم سواء كنت عندهم عند قبورهم أو خارجها هم لا يسمعون لكنهم ينتفعون ولا فرق فالدعاء يصل سواء كان من قريب أو من بعيد في الليل و في النهار في أي مكان كنت.أما الزيارة البدعية التي يفعلها الناس للذهاب إلى القبور والكلام عندها و التردد عليها والوقوف على الأجداث بل ورفع الحوائج إليها فهذا لا شك من الشرك البين وكذلك من هذا التوسل بأعمال الأشخاص الآخرين فهذا لا يحل لك فإنما يحل لك أن تتوسل بأعمالك أنت لأنك إنما تسأل الله بشيء قدمته أنت لأنك لا يمكن أن تتوسل إليه بعمل شخص آخر يستحقه ذالك الشخص فإنما يوفي العامل أجره فكل إنسان يمكن أن يتوسل بعمل عمله هو أخلص فيه لله لكن لا يمكن أن يتوسل بعمل شخص آخر أبدا فهذا الأخ عليه أن يتوب إلى الله مما مضى وأن يترك التوسل بأعمال أشخاص آخرين لم يعملها هو و أن يحافظ على الجد و العهد كما أمر وعلى التوحيد والفرائض وأن يتعلم العلم فهذا خير له وهذا الذي يلتزم به سنة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم. (و عموما فإن التوسل صريح في الفقه و ليس في العقائد)
body_en:
QUESTION: I submitted a request to one of the shaykhs to be admitted to his Sufi order (ṭarīqah), and he granted it to me together with conditions, among them: taking the matter in earnest, keeping the covenant, keeping it secret, not breaching the condition, not breaching the oneness of God (tawḥīd), and not breaching the obligatory duties (farāʾiḍ). I am without knowledge of the sacred sciences. So I remained on that footing, on the path and in the service of the shaykh, until he died. I then grew accustomed to visiting with reverence and with supplication, and after that I seek nearness to God by his righteous deeds, just as I used to seek nearness through him while he was alive, in order to gain benefits and remove harms. Is this from the sunnah, or is it associating partners with God (shirk) — may God protect us from it?

ANSWER: These counsels the shaykh gave him are unobjectionable. A person must take the matter in earnest, must fulfil the covenant, must likewise not breach the oneness of God nor the obligatory duties, and must learn sacred knowledge. These are counsels that the shaykh is obliged to give, and the one counselled is obliged to be counselled with them always.

For the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: «Religion is sincere counsel.» We said: 'To whom?' He said: «To God, to His Book, to His Messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims, and to the generality of them.»

As for what he mentioned about being without knowledge: the mere formulae of remembrance that he performs are no substitute for seeking sacred knowledge. Rather, a person is bound to learn what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, brought — for it may be that what he is doing is in the first place contrary to what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, brought. So let him search out what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, brought; let him act by it; and let him make it the judge over everything besides it. If what the shaykh or anyone else ordered agrees with what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, brought, then let a person act by it, because the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, ordered him to. And if it is contrary to anything the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, brought, then let him throw it back at whoever said it, whoever that may be; and let him not be ashamed to reject from anyone something that contradicts what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, brought — even if it be a father, or a shaykh, or an elder. It is not possible for you to accept from anyone at all what is contrary to what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, brought.

As for what this person does after the death of the shaykh mentioned, by way of visiting: visiting graves is recommended (mandūb) in general for Muslims, so as to call the hereafter to mind. But the one visited derives no benefit from it, does not perceive it, does not feel it at all, hears nothing of what the visitor says, and cannot benefit him with anything: he does not lift any harm from him nor bring him any benefit, and there is no relation at all between the two. Rather you take admonition from his bones, which the earth consumes; you take admonition from his private affairs and his wealth, which have become the property of someone else; and you take admonition from his family, who used to think that he benefited them and saw to their affairs, and he has gone from them and has done them no harm at all. This is what accrues to you from visiting any grave whatsoever. Visiting graves — whether those in them are people of faith or people of unbelief, people of uprightness or people of open sin, whether you know them or do not know them — leads to this calling to mind, the calling to mind of the hereafter, and this is what is sought from it. As for the dead, they benefit in their graves only from supplication: that you supplicate for them. And when you supplicate for them, whether you are beside them at their graves or away from them, they do not hear — but they benefit, and there is no difference. The supplication reaches them, whether from near or from far, by night or by day, in whatever place you are.

As for the innovated visitation that people perform — going to the graves, speaking at them, frequenting them, standing over the tombs, and even raising their needs to them — this is without doubt manifest associating of partners with God (shirk). And of this same kind is seeking nearness by the deeds of other persons: this is not lawful for you. What is lawful for you is only to seek nearness by your own deeds, because you are asking God by something that you yourself have put forward; for you cannot seek nearness to Him by the deed of another person, since that person is the one entitled to it — for it is the doer who is paid his wage in full. So every person may seek nearness by a deed that he himself has done and in which he was sincere for God; but he can never seek nearness by the deed of another person. So this brother must repent to God for what has passed, must abandon seeking nearness by the deeds of other persons which he did not himself do, must keep to earnestness and to the covenant as he was ordered, and to the oneness of God and the obligatory duties, and must learn sacred knowledge. This is better for him, and this is what adheres to the sunnah of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace.

(And in general, tawassul belongs properly to jurisprudence (fiqh) and not to the articles of creed.)

flags.arabic: و عموما فإن التوسل صريح في الفقه و ليس في العقائد
options: And in general, tawassul belongs properly to jurisprudence (fiqh) and not to the articles of creed.
And in general, tawassul is treated explicitly in the books of jurisprudence and not in the works of creed.
And in general, the question of tawassul is a clear-cut matter of jurisprudence rather than of creed.
flags.note: HIGH SIGNIFICANCE. صريح can mean 'belongs properly / is strictly' or 'is explicitly treated'. On reading 0 the Sheikh is placing the whole tawassul dispute outside creed — a substantive position with real consequences, since it bears on whether error in it touches a person's belief. On reading 1 he is only remarking where the topic is discussed in the literature. The two are not equivalent and the translator cannot settle between them. The Sheikh's office should confirm.

flags.context: لقد قدمت لأحد المشايخ طلبا لطريقته فأعطانيها مصحوبة بشروط
options: a request to be admitted to his Sufi order (ṭarīqah)
a request for his ṭarīqah (spiritual path)
a request for his method of devotion
flags.note: The conditions the questioner describes — a covenant, secrecy, a bond of service to the shaykh until his death — are the marks of initiation into a Sufi ṭarīqah. Option 2 is neutral but loses the institutional sense on which the question turns. The Sheikh himself does not name the order, and does not comment on ṭarīqah affiliation as such; nothing to that effect has been added.

flags.arabic: ويجب أيضا على المنصوح أن ينصح بها دائما
flags.context: فهذه النصائح تجب على الشيخ أن ينصح بها ويجب أيضا على المنصوح أن ينصح بها دائما
options: and the one counselled is obliged to be counselled with them always
and the one counselled is obliged to pass them on as counsel always
and the one counselled is obliged to keep being reminded of them
flags.note: The verb ينصح is used twice with different subjects and the second is ambiguous between passive ('be counselled') and active ('give counsel'). The sentence as printed is awkward and may be a transcription slip from a spoken original. Rendered literally; a reviewer with the audio should resolve it.

translator_notes: This is a complete written fatwa: the questioner's account followed by the Sheikh's answer. The two are not separated by any marker in the Arabic source — the answer begins at إن هذه النصائح. The labels QUESTION and ANSWER have been added in the English for legibility and are editorial, not the Sheikh's.

Rulings actually given here, with their exact force: visiting graves in general is 'recommended' (mandūb); the innovated visitation described is 'without doubt manifest shirk'; seeking nearness through another person's deeds is 'not lawful for you'. None has been strengthened or softened, and no ruling word has been supplied where he used none.
The hadith «Religion is sincere counsel» is given without a named collection; none has been added.
The source spells ذلك as ذالك throughout and omits some spaces (e.g. كنت.أما); body_ar preserves the source exactly.
